text: Murder Holes
Crackday Chevelier was a crusader castle in the Holy Land that had never fallen, not to
Saladin, not to anyone who came for it.
Then, in 1271, a Muslim Sultan named Bybars arrived.
He had been working through the crusader's castles like a to-do list, one after another.
Crack would not be crossing off by storm.
The only way in ran through a stone corridor hundreds of feet long bent back on itself,
with a gallery running along the top.
The floor of that gallery was open.
On purpose, the corridor was built to let attackers in, pack them tight, and drop things
on them from above until nobody was moving.
Not the boiling oil of the movies, which was rare and costly, but rock boiling water and
heated sand.
They called them Murder Holes.
So Bybars did not bother with the front door.
He preferred to make his own.
He stood off and hammered the walls with siege engines for weeks, until he had knocked a
fresh hole through a tower and sent his men in through that instead.
The garrison, maybe 60 nights, fell back into the inner castle.
He could not get them out of that either.
So the castle the Sultan could not storm, did not fall to a storm.
It fell to a con.
Bybars had a letter forged, dressed up as an order from the night's own commander, telling
the last defenders to give up.
It was, more or less, a medieval fishing scam.
The most feared knights in the crusader world read the fake memo, believed it, and opened
the gates.
They had held off Saladin.
They had held off an army for a month.
They could not hold off bad paperwork.
The Murder Holes had done their job.
Nobody wanted to walk under them, not even Bybars.
Moat.
The longest siege in medieval England was, in the end, a war against a lake.
In 1265, the Barons who had risen against King Henry III were crushed at the Battle of
Yvesham, their leader Simon de Montfort killed.
The survivors fell back to a castle called Kenilworth.
Refused every demand to surrender, and dared the king to come and take it.
He came.
He would spend the next six months learning that he could not.
Kenilworth sat in the middle of a lake.
Its builders had dammed the local streams into a great artificial mirror.
Hundreds of yards of open water wrapped all the way around the walls.
Siege engines could not get close enough to hit anything.
And no one could tunnel, because everything underground was water.
The most powerful army in England had shown up to attack a very large pond.
The king tried everything anyway.
He sent to London for the largest trebuchets in the kingdom, which flung their stones mostly
into the lake.
He had barges dragged over land from Chester for a night assault, and the garrison drove
them back.
When a cardinal arrived to excommunicate the rebels from a safe hillside, they dressed one
of their own men in white, and had him excommunicate the king, the cardinal, and the whole royal army
right back.
It was, more or less, a medieval flame war, and the castle was winning it.
The water never broke.
What finally took Kenowarth was not an army, but an empty larder.
After roughly six months, hunger and disease did what the trebuchets could not.
The lake had held the whole time.
The men behind it just ran out of food.
Port Colus.
Everyone knows what a port Colus does.
The heroes sprint through the gate.
The iron grill comes crashing down behind them, and some slower soldier gets caught underneath.
The most dramatic door in history.
It is also mostly a lie.
In real sieges, a dropped port Colus almost never does the thing the movies love.
No castle was ever won or lost because a grill dropped and squished an army in the gateway.
There is no great massacre in the gatehouse anyone can point to.
Most of the time it just sat there, lowered.
Being a really good door.
A door with a great publicist.
And that was the genius.
It was a grill, not a slab, so defenders could shoot out through the gaps while nothing got
in.
It dropped faster than any hinged gate could swing, and it did not burn.
It was the fire door of the medieval castle.
Deeply unglamorous and the only reason anyone inside kept breathing.
The famous killing version, the one that crushes some poor man in the archway, spent almost
its whole career waiting for a moment that never came.
Most attackers took one look at a lowered port Colus and went off to dig at the walls
instead.
The trap was real.
It just never got the memo it was supposed to be scary.
Arrow loops.
An army marched up to the walls of Carcassonne to take the city and never reached them.
It should have been easy.
Carcassonne belonged by right to the man leading that army, Raymond Tranquaval, whose family
had held it for a century until a crusade took it and gave it to the king of France.
In 1240 he came back to claim it, with soldiers at his back and only a small royal garrison
in his way.
He should have walked in.
He got nowhere.
The walls of Carcassonne were pierced top to bottom with narrow vertical slits.
From outside, each was a line in the stone barely wider than a hand.
From inside, it opened into a wide alcove where a crossbow man could stand in near total cover
and sweep the ground below.
They were called arrow loops and they were, in effect, a one-way window with a crossbow
behind it.
The man at the slit could see everything and be hit by almost nothing.
The man in the field faced a wall full of slots, any one of which might be aimed at him.
Tranquaval's army had crossbow men by the hundred.
Guillaume des Ormes, the Seneschal holding the city, wrote to the queen of France that
the enemy had so many that no one could step outside the walls without being hit.
It was a storm of bolts and the garrison held anyway.
They shot from the slits while the attackers stood exposed below.
A handful of men behind arrow loops could hold a wall against an army and at Carcassonne
they did.
Tranquaval besieged his own city for weeks and never broke in.
When a royal army marched up to relieve it, he gave up and rode away.
He never got Carcassonne back and, in time, surrendered his family's claim to it for good.
A hundred years of inheritance and a slit the width of his hand was all that stood between
him and it.
It was enough.
Round Towers.
King John needed pigs.
Not to eat.
November 1215, he sent an urgent order to his Justish Yarr, 40 of the fattest pigs that
could be found.
The ones least good for eating, delivered day and night with all speed.
It was also how he meant to bring down a castle.
The castle was Rochester, held against him by rebel barons in the war that broke out
after Magna Carta.
Its keep was one of the tallest in England and for weeks John Stone Throwers had battered
it with nothing to show.
So he stopped throwing stones at the tower and started digging under it.
His miners tunneled beneath the square corner of the keep, propping the tunnel with timber
as they went.
Then they packed the props with the fattest of 40 pigs and set it alight.
The fire ate through the wood.
The tunnel collapsed and the entire corner of the great keep came down with it.
That collapse taught everyone watching a lesson.
A square tower has corners and a corner is a weakness.
The one place a miner can dig out from two sides at once.
Where a wall is easiest to drop.
So when Rochester's fallen corner was rebuilt, it was not rebuilt square.
It was rebuilt round.
A round tower gives a miner no corner to attack and shrugs off blows that would shatter an
angle and round towers already on the rise became the shape of the serious castle.
Rochester did not invent the idea, but it made the case about as loudly as a case can be made.
The garrison did not even surrender when the corner fell.
They pulled back behind a wall inside the keep and held on until the food ran out and
the corner they had lost was rebuilt curved so that no one could ever again do to it what
a few dozen pigs had done once.
Drawbridge
The bridge is rising.
The hero makes the leap.
The men chasing him do not and they drop screaming into the moat below.
It is the best three seconds in any castle film.
It is also almost pure invention.
Here is what a drawbridge actually was.
The first castles sat behind a ditch or a moat and the only way to reach the gate was
a wooden bridge laid across it.
That bridge could be hauled up on chains so that when it rose the crossing simply vanished
and in real sieges it rarely got the cinematic moment.
No army was famously destroyed because a bridge went up at exactly the right second.
Most of the time it did the least heroic job imaginable down in the morning to let the millers
cart in up at night to keep everyone out.
It was for most of its life a very large garage door.
The clever part was quieter.
Raised, the bridge did not just close the crossing.
It swung up flush against the gate and became part of the wall.
A slab of oak with no footing left below to bring a ram up at all.
The genius of the drawbridge was never that it dropped men into a pit.
It was that it could make the way in simply stop existing.
The dramatic version, the one that lifts at the last second and sends men into the water
was mostly a story.
The real drawbridge spent its career letting the groceries through.
Its finest hour was doing nothing at all.
Sitting there, raised being a wall.
Gatehouse.
On Castle in England was worth more than any other because it sat at the shortest crossing
from the continent.
Whoever held it held the door to the entire country.
It was Dover and in 1216 with England in revolt against King John.
A French prince named Louis landed on the coast and marched straight for it.
He came far closer to taking it than the English would ever like to admit.
Louis went straight for the Great North Gatehouse.
The strongest point in the whole castle.
That sounds backwards.
But the gatehouse was the only real way in.
Everything else was a solid wall.
So his miners took the outer defenses, tunneled under a gate tower and burned away the props
holding their tunnel up.
The tower cracked and came down and a hole opened straight into Dover.
French soldiers poured through the gap and this is the moment Dover should have fallen.
Instead, the garrison under a night named Hubert de Berg met them in the breach, fought
them back out by hand and jammed the gap shut with timber torn from their own castle.
Louis had broken the gate of Dover.
He still could not get through it.
The near-miss terrified the English and their answer was drastic.
They bricked the North Gate up into a solid block of stone and built a new entrance elsewhere.
It was less a door than a checkpoint designed to kill.
A passage that bent so no ram could charge it, ran beneath holes for dropping things on
whoever stood below and could be sealed with grill after grill.
That is the kind of near-disaster that turned the castle gate into the most overbuilt door
in the building.
Somewhere, once, someone had almost lost a kingdom through a simple one.
Concentric walls.
Richard the Lionheart, King of England, built one castle he loved above all the rest.
It was called Chateau Gyard and it stood on a cliff above the river Seine guarding Normandy,
England's lands in France against the French King who wanted them back.
Richard raised it at astonishing speed, wrapped it in ring after ring of wall and reportedly
called it his fair one-year-old daughter.
He was certain no one could ever take it.
He was almost right.
The genius was in the walls.
Guy Lard did not have one wall but several, setting one inside the next like the rings
of a target.
Break through the outer wall and an attacker did not find the castle.
He found himself in a narrow yard trapped between the wall he had just breached and a
taller one ahead with defenders firing down from both sides.
A breach did not get him in.
It got him killed.
So when Philip, the King of France, came for it in 1203, he did not try to smash straight
through.
He settled in for a siege that ground on through the winter.
These miners brought down part of the outer wall and the inner rings held exactly as Richard
had built them to.
Then a handful of Philip's men found the one thing the design had not accounted for.
A toilet shaft ran from a chapel in the middle ward down to the outside of the wall.
They climbed up it, came out inside the castle and threw the way open.
The castle Richard swore could never fall was open from the inside.
The garrison surrendered and with Guy Lard gone, nothing stood between Philip and Normandy.
Within months he had taken Ruol and the rest of it.
Richard had built rings of wall no army could break and every one of them held.
It made no difference.
His masterpiece and with it an empire his family had held in France for nearly 140 years was
lost through a hole built for going to the toilet.
